articles.full_text:
JOHOR BARU: A Malaysian plantation group and several Singapore-linked companies have been linked to Indonesian concessions where fire hotspots were detected.
Indonesian authorities have not disclosed the identities or nationalities of the 19 companies investigated over fires that burned 11,047ha across seven provinces.
A report by Greenpeace Indonesia, Greenpeace Malaysia and Pantau Gambut identified at least one Malaysian company alongside four concessions linked to Singapore-based companies.
The findings, released on Oct 5, however, did not directly blame them for starting the fires in Sumatra and West Kalimantan, or committing any offence.
Indonesian Consul-General in Johor Baru Sigit Suryantoro Widiyanto said they identified 57 businesses across eight provinces in their enforcement crackdown.
What To Read Next
Indonesia's Environment Ministry had linked the businesses to open burning covering 33,514ha.
Authorities recorded 97 police reports involving corporations and were investigating 46 suspects, including five companies.
The Forestry Ministry imposed administrative sanctions on 26 companies, including revoking five permits, suspending 13 and issuing written warnings or restoration orders to eight.
On Thursday, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto had agreed to address the worsening haze, as Malaysia renewed calls for stronger regional cooperation.
Meanwhile, Sari Wilson-Pohan, an Indonesian who has lived in Johor since 2014, said she was embarrassed and saddened by what she viewed as a lack of urgency by Indonesia in addressing the fires. Both her sons attend school in Johor and her husband works in Singapore.
"Regardless of who owns the companies, Indonesia must put humanity first. Protecting people, the environment and our future should always come before protecting big businesses," she told the New Straits Times.
She said she had submitted an open letter to Prabowo urging decisive action and accountability.
"Enough is enough. People must come before profits."

articles.title: Rare red carpet in KL for Myanmar's leader sparks outrage, but signals shifting Asean stance - The Business Times
articles.summary: Rare red carpet in KL for Myanmar's leader sparks outrage, but signals shifting Asean stance  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
Myanmar could test whether the South-east Asian block can distinguish necessary diplomatic engagement from full political normalisation
[BANGKOK] Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing has wrapped up an official two-day visit to Malaysia – his fifth to a regional country in 2026 – amid outcry against Putrajaya for welcoming him without extracting commitments on ending violence.
During his visit that wrapped up on Thursday (Oct 8), he met Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and both agreed on advancing cooperation in sectors like education, energy and healthcare. However, no pacts were inked.
“I firmly believe that enhancing our bilateral economic cooperation will bring highly practical economic benefits and joint opportunities for the people of both countries,” Min Aung Hlaing said in a joint press conference on Thursday.
“I also wish to invite Malaysian business leaders from various sectors to come and invest in Myanmar, a country that has excellent investment opportunities,” he added.
Since Min Aung Hlaing assumed the presidency in April after a carefully orchestrated election held from December to January 2026, he has visited Asean states Laos, Thailand, Vietnam and Cambodia.
But the visit to Malaysia has raised eyebrows especially given that Putrajaya used to be one of the harshest critics of the coup carried out by the Myanmar military regime in 2021.
Since the February 2021 coup which Min Aung Hlaing staged, Asean has barred him from all leaders’ summits. However, half of the 11-member Asean group have now laid out the red carpet for him, normalising ties with the former junta leader.
Repatriation high on the agenda
In Kuala Lumpur though, the repatriation of Myanmar nationals was high on the agenda with more expected to be sent back.
During the same press conference, Anwar praised Min Aung Hlaing for being “very cooperative” on the matter.
“Many of us do not realise that hardly any country in my experience are willing to accept this repatriation in large numbers at their own expense as you have shown,” Anwar said.
But to Rohingya activist and former Myanmar political prisoner Wai Wai Nu, “the plan is not just morally bankrupt but it makes no practical sense”.
“Deporting refugees to Myanmar under an agreement with Min Aung Hlaing is a violation of international law and against the fundamental principle of non-refoulement,” she said.
Currently, the western Rakhine state where most of the Rohingya refugees are from is largely under the control of ethnic Arakan Army and not the military regime.
“The (repatriation) plan will fail while emboldening Min Aung Hlaing and fuelling instability, making a lasting solution harder to reach,” Wai Wai Nu added.
Matthew Smith, chief executive officer and founder of civil society Fortify Rights, said that welcoming Min Aung Hlaing while returning Myanmar nationals “sends a devastating and wrong message”.
According to the Institute for Strategy and Policy-Myanmar, an independent think-tank based in Thailand, the military conducted at least 1,583 aerial attacks in just five months from Mar 31 to Aug 31 in 2026.
Rights groups chastise the visit
Malaysia’s engagement with Min Aung Hlaing has outraged rights activists, with Charles Santiago, co-chair of Asean Parliamentarians for Human Rights saying the visit “has legitimised” the Myanmar leader’s political status and was “a win” for him.
“Diplomacy is not merely about having a conversation. It is about leverage, accountability, consequences and outcomes. Why should we believe that another bilateral conversation will succeed where years of Asean engagement have failed?” Santiago asked.
Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of ALTSEAN-Burma, an advocacy and rights non-government organisation based in Thailand called the visit “a significant sell-out by Malaysia”.
This came after Malaysian Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan told the Parliament on Jun 25 that Kuala Lumpur does not recognise Myanmar’s post-election administration.
“I have already stated that we do not recognise them. When we do not recognise them, the term ‘government’ does not apply from Malaysia’s perspective,” he had insisted.
However, on Thursday, Malaysia’s Anwar changed his tone.
“We, of course, are reminded of the Asean mechanism but we also understand that the President and your government have made a lot of efforts in order to enhance better relations but to have the necessary reform, policy changes, adjustments in your own country,” Anwar said.
“We, on our part in Malaysia, will do whatever is possible to make sure that we enhance this collaboration and ultimately take Myanmar as part of our community of nations without prejudice and particularly in the context of Asean,” he added.
Stothard added that repatriating Myanmar citizens boycotting tax payments to the junta, and replacing them with the regime’s approved batch of documented Myanmar workers to Malaysia, is another way the military-linked government seeks to earn tax revenue.
Focus on repatriation scale
The repatriation of almost 200,000 Myanmar nationals living in Malaysia including Rohingya Muslims, a stateless minority, is a major topic between the two nations.
During the press conference, both leaders said their respective ministries will coordinate the deportation process.
“We will expedite the process to bring them back and we are sending one naval ship to Malaysia for their repatriation,” said Min Aung Hlaing.
The Rohingya have long been discriminated against in Myanmar and a brutal military crackdown in 2017 forced at least 700,000 to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh, where they now live in the world’s largest refugee camp.
Anwar previously said no Rohingya Muslims have been repatriated so far, even as he informed the Malaysian Parliament on Tuesday that more than 10,000 Myanmar nationals have been sent home since January 2026.
And just a week before Min Aung Hlaing’s visit, Malaysia deported almost 2,000 Myanmar nationals on Sep 29.
Analysts said this move serves Anwar’s political survival, as Malaysians’ resentment towards this group swells.
“Anwar’s metric at this stage is how to win Malay votes because he has been losing popularity ahead of Malaysia’s expected general election,” said Stothard.
Meanwhile, Khoo Ying Hooi, an associate professor of international relations and human rights at Universiti Malaya’s Department of International and Strategic Studies, described the deportation as problematic.
Though Myanmar has given the assurance that the returnees will be safe and protected, she said sending them back to a country that is still engaged in active violent conflicts is worrying.
Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, an independent global conflict monitor, reported that since the coup, at least 100,000 people have died. The deportees also risk being subjected to forced conscription by the junta.
Khoo said Malaysia needs to extract more tangible commitments from Myanmar such as allowing independent monitoring and clear procedures for identifying people who require international protection.
“Malaysia could also use the meeting to press for humanitarian access and some demonstrable movement on the broader Asean agenda,” she suggested.
Asean peace plan weakens
Asean maintains its ban on Min Aung Hlaing and expects him to substantially implement the 2021 Five-Point Consensus (5PC), which includes ending violence and allowing greater humanitarian aid delivery access among other conditions before reinstating his participation.
But Min Aung Hlaing has largely disregarded the peace plan, claiming Myanmar’s pro-military parliamentarians have rejected it.
The two leaders made no mention of the 5PC when making statements at the joint press conference.
As recently as Sep 28, the Myanmar military reportedly conducted an air strike on a market in western Rakhine state, killing some 50 civilians.
“When relatively limited concessions receive prominent diplomatic recognition while mass civilian casualties produce a much weaker collective political response, Asean risks appearing to lower its own benchmark for progress,” Khoo said.
“That is particularly problematic because cessation of violence is at the heart of the Five-Point Consensus,” she added.
Independent Myanmar analyst Wai Yan Phyo Naing said the bilateral visits also send a wrong message to the wider global community. He said nations may use political justification as an excuse to restore diplomatic contact without requiring meaningful concessions from the junta.
“Such engagement would further legitimise Min Aung Hlaing, weaken international pressure, and marginalise Myanmar’s democratic forces. It is particularly dangerous because the junta may interpret normalisation as evidence that violence and repression have no serious diplomatic consequences,” said Wai Yan Phyo Naing.
Myanmar, Khoo said, will be a major test for Asean on whether the grouping can distinguish between necessary diplomatic engagement and full political normalisation.
“One visit becomes several visits, and eventually the argument shifts from whether governments should engage Min Aung Hlaing to why they should continue isolating him when his own neighbours no longer do so,” she said. THE STRAITS TIMES

articles.title: Philippine president Marcos looks to Singapore to build on ASEAN digital pact amid US-China rivalry - The Straits Times
articles.summary: Philippine president Marcos looks to Singapore to build on ASEAN digital pact amid US-China rivalry  The Straits Times
articles.full_text:
AI generated
SINGAPORE – Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr is counting on Singapore to turn ASEAN’s landmark digital economy agreement into reality when it takes over the regional grouping’s chairmanship in 2027, with artificial intelligence (AI) a key priority.
Marcos said the Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), which ASEAN is expected to formally sign in November under Manila’s chairmanship, would lay the groundwork for closer digital integration across South-east Asia.
“With the DEFA in place, with the road map in place, I’m hoping Singapore will pick up the ball, and I know that they will pick up the ball and run with it,” he told The Straits Times in an exclusive interview on Oct 8.
The aim, he said, was to make the agreement “more than just a road map” for ASEAN and its dealings with the rest of the world, particularly in AI.
The 69-year-old son of the late strongman Ferdinand Marcos Sr is in Singapore on a five-day working visit from Oct 7 to 11, during which he is meeting political and business leaders to deepen economic cooperation between the two countries.
His remarks come as South-east Asia seeks to tap the economic potential of AI while navigating growing competition between the United States and China over advanced technologies and their supply chains.
Dealing with AI, the elephant in the room
Marcos said he had discussed with Prime Minister Lawrence Wong the importance of ensuring that regional initiatives continued beyond the one-year chairmanship of any single ASEAN member state.

He recalled a similar conversation with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim before the Philippines assumed the chairmanship, during which Anwar encouraged him to pursue agreements that might take several years to implement.
The DEFA, one of the Philippines’ major priorities as ASEAN chair, seeks to establish common rules for digital trade, cross-border data flows, electronic payments and other aspects of the digital economy.
Marcos said Singapore, which he described as a regional leader in digitalisation and AI, was well placed to lead the next stage of implementation.
“You and I both know that that is now the elephant in the room: It’s AI and how you deal with it, how you take advantage of it, how you safeguard against the dangers of it,” he said.
He also hoped Singapore will use its position as a regional financial and commercial hub to boost trade among ASEAN economies.
The Philippine leader noted that intra-ASEAN trade accounts for only about 24% of the grouping’s total trade, leaving considerable room for the region to strengthen its internal market.
Closer economic integration has become more important, he said, as the region grapples with Covid-19-related disruptions, wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, and shifts in US trade policy.
But as ASEAN embraces AI, Marcos acknowledged that the technology would inevitably reshape labour markets and put jobs at risk.
He said governments must invest in retraining workers and work closely with the private sector to ensure that training programmes meet industry needs.
The Philippines, with its large overseas workforce, is particularly vulnerable to shifts in the global job market.
Marcos said his administration has rolled out social support programmes to help workers transition to new jobs.
“While they are still transitioning, while they are still in training, while they are not yet working, the government is there to continue to support them,” he said.
Expanding Singapore-Philippines ties
Beyond ASEAN, Marcos hopes to deepen economic ties with Singapore in emerging industries, including AI, healthcare and digital infrastructure, and to establish partnerships that will outlast his presidency, which ends in 2028.
Singapore is the second-largest foreign investor in the Philippines, just behind South Korea. But Singapore and the Philippines are now exploring opportunities in sectors where Singaporean companies have traditionally had less involvement, such as healthcare and the digital economy.
Marcos attributed the growing interest in part to his administration’s efforts to attract foreign businesses to the Philippines. “We have worked very hard to make the Philippines a more investment-friendly destination,” he said.
He cited changes to foreign ownership restrictions in selected industries, longer land leases, tax incentives and efforts to improve the ease of doing business.
He said foreign investors had been reluctant to commit to long-term projects in the Philippines because they lacked assurances that they could remain in the country long enough to recover their investments.
Marcos had in 2025 signed a law allowing foreign investors to lease land in the Philippines for up to 99 years, replacing the old policy of an initial 50-year lease with a one-time renewal of up to 25 years.
In 2026, he signed an executive order allowing 100% foreign ownership in renewable energy projects and certain sectors like airports, railways, expressways and transport services.
Foreign ownership of telecommunications services is also permitted at up to 100% where reciprocity exists, while foreign equity in smaller retail enterprises is capped at 40%.
His administration has also encouraged public-private partnerships and joint ventures to attract investments in major infrastructure projects.
Marcos said the goal was to encourage foreign companies to make long-term commitments rather than seek quick profits.
Looking towards the end of his term in 2028, he said he hoped the basic elements of a business-friendly environment would be firmly in place by then.
He also backed the prospect of a potential ASEAN-European Union free trade agreement, saying the Philippines-EU trade pact, signed in September, could help pave the way for a broader region-to-region deal. “The Philippines’ free trade agreement with the EU is going to be very, very important,” he said, adding that it could open up new markets for Filipino businesses.
He said such bilateral pacts would be increasingly important as countries sought to protect their economies from global uncertainty.

articles.title: The Ministry of Industry and Trade aims for exports to exceed $1.041 billion, more than double the 2025 figure. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The Ministry of Industry and Trade aims for exports to exceed $1.041 billion, more than double the 2025 figure.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
At the consultation workshop on the Strategy for Import and Export of Goods until 2030, with a vision to 2045, held on October 9th, Ms. Nguyen Cam Trang, representative of the Import and Export Department ( Ministry of Industry and Trade ), stated that in the context of the Government setting a target of double-digit economic growth, exports continue to be one of the important driving forces. Therefore, the export growth target for the coming period needs to be redefined to suit the new development requirements.
 Accordingly, the draft Strategy for Import and Export of Goods until 2030, with a vision to 2045, aims to promote high growth in import and export, contributing to the double-digit economic growth target for the period 2026-2030; while also shifting strongly from extensive to intensive growth, enhancing the added value, productivity, and competitiveness of Vietnamese goods.
 The target is to achieve an average annual growth rate of 15-16% in merchandise exports during the 2026-2030 period, and an average annual growth rate of 12-13% in imports. The trade balance aims for a sustainable surplus, with the proportion of export surplus to total export value averaging 3-6% during this period.
 By 2045, Vietnam aims to be among the top 10 countries in the world in terms of export and import turnover; with a trade surplus of 7-10%. 
 One of the key objectives is to enhance the role of domestic enterprises and increase the processing and technological content in export goods. Accordingly, the proportion of export turnover from the domestic enterprise sector in the total national export turnover is targeted to reach approximately 28-30% by 2030, increasing to 38-40% by 2045.
 The proportion of processed or refined goods in total export turnover is expected to reach 89-90% by 2030 and over 92% by 2045.
 The target is to increase the proportion of high-tech product exports in the total value of processed and manufactured goods exports to approximately 50% by 2030 and over 55% by 2045.
 Regarding trade scale, the draft presents growth scenarios up to 2030. Specifically, in the medium scenario, export turnover is expected to reach US$953.7 billion by 2030; the high scenario targets US$1,041.1 billion, while the low scenario is US$765 billion.
 According to statistics from the Customs Department, Vietnam's total export turnover in 2025 will only reach US$475.06 billion and US$434.32 billion in the first nine months of 2026. Compared to 2025, to achieve the 2030 target, export turnover under the high-scenario must increase by an additional US$566.04 billion, equivalent to approximately 2.19 times. In the medium-scenario, the increase is US$478.64 billion; while in the low-scenario, it is US$289.94 billion.
 Mr. Nguyen Hoai Nam, General Secretary of the Vietnam Association of Seafood Processing and Export, believes that the strategy needs to clearly define objectives, resources, and specific solutions. Tasks should be concretized into action programs, with implementation roadmaps and coordination among ministries, sectors, localities, and relevant units.
 According to him, Vietnam has potential in terms of raw materials, but to improve its position in the international market, it cannot rely solely on existing advantages. Businesses need to enhance processing, improve quality, meet customer requirements, and increase product value.
 He noted that the feasibility of the Strategy depends not only on defining objectives but also on the ability to overcome bottlenecks during implementation. The responsibilities of each ministry and sector need to be clarified, especially regarding issues related to raw material supply, quality management, and market development. 
 In the first nine months of 2026, Vietnam had a trade deficit of $19.39 billion. Photo: Hoang Ha
 Mr. Pham Van Quan, Deputy Director of the Department of Industry, suggested that the strategy should focus on programs to develop supporting industries and assist manufacturing enterprises in participating more deeply in global supply chains. This is an important direction to gradually reduce dependence on imported raw materials and components, improve domestic production capacity, and increase the ability to control various stages in the value chain.
 Deputy Minister of Industry and Trade Luong Hoang Thai emphasized that import and export are important driving forces contributing to Vietnam's achievement of development goals. In some periods, exports and foreign investment have played a leading role in economic growth.
 However, the Deputy Minister also pointed out that in the past, the import-export strategy focused heavily on the goal of increasing volume. When the economy is still small, the development of manufacturing industries needs to rely on the global market and economy, thereby creating momentum for growth.
 However, after a period of development, the scale of the Vietnamese economy has grown larger, and the level of trade openness is high. Accordingly, the new context requires a shift in focus from quantitative growth to improving the quality and efficiency of import and export activities.
 "Therefore, the import-export strategy needs to orient Vietnam to participate more deeply in essential stages, while creating connections with science , technology, and industrial development strategies. Through this, import-export activities will not only expand in scale but also contribute to improving production capacity and ensuring a stable and long-term balance of payments," the Deputy Minister noted.
 Accordingly, the Ministry of Industry and Trade will continue to listen to feedback, gather opinions, and refine the draft Strategy before submitting it to the Prime Minister for consideration and decision on its promulgation.

articles.title: Imports and exports exceed $888 billion: How can Vietnamese businesses benefit more? - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Imports and exports exceed $888 billion: How can Vietnamese businesses benefit more?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
From increasing export turnover to enhancing added value.
 Speaking at the seminar "Improving the quality of import and export growth in the process of restructuring the Industry and Trade sector" on October 9th, Ms. Trinh Thi Thu Hien, Deputy Director of the Import and Export Department ( Ministry of Industry and Trade ), stated that the total import and export turnover of goods in Vietnam in the first nine months of 2026 reached over 888 billion USD, an increase of 30.4% compared to the same period last year.
 Specifically, exports reached over $434 billion, an increase of 24.5%; imports reached over $453 billion, an increase of 36.7%. The fact that imports increased faster than exports indicates expanding demand for inputs to serve production, while also highlighting the need to improve domestic supply capacity to increase the value created from trade activities.
 The export structure continues to shift towards an increased proportion of processed and manufactured industrial goods. Computers, electronic products, machinery, telephones, and components remain important product groups.
 On the import side, production materials reached US$426.92 billion, accounting for 94.1% of the total import value. Of this, machinery, equipment, tools, and spare parts accounted for 58.3%; raw materials, fuels, and other materials accounted for 35.8%.
 "Therefore, for both export and import goods, we are currently importing mainly raw materials to serve production," Ms. Hien stated. 
 According to experts, the key to successful import and export activities is increasing value.
 The large proportion of production materials indicates that imports play a crucial role in production and export activities. However, to improve the quality of growth, the issue is not just about expanding the scale of imports or exports, but also about the ability to transform machinery, raw materials, and technology into higher-value products, while increasing the value created by domestic enterprises.
 According to Mr. Phan Duc Hieu, a member of the 16th National Assembly and a member of the National Assembly's Economic and Financial Committee, a crucial requirement for import and export activities is to increase value, especially for domestic businesses. To achieve this, Vietnamese businesses need to participate more deeply in global value chains, increase their ability to supply raw materials to manufacturing and export businesses, and enhance their capacity to directly participate more in domestic and international economic activities.
 The policies and guidelines are relatively clear, but it is crucial to translate them into concrete implementation programs. Besides refining policies, it is necessary to promote connections between domestic and foreign businesses, while also supporting the enhancement of production capacity.
 "Essentially, exporting or importing is not just about expanding markets, but first and foremost about the capacity to produce truly high-quality and competitive products. Therefore, programs to improve production capacity should be considered a fundamental solution," Mr. Hieu emphasized.
 In the context of Vietnam's high growth targets, the need for investment in machinery, equipment, and production materials also opens up opportunities to develop domestic production capacity. Therefore, long-term solutions are needed to transform the opportunities arising from imports into a driving force for enhancing the capacity of Vietnamese businesses.
 Developing supporting industries and increasing linkages with FDI.
 The electronics industry clearly demonstrates this challenge. It is a highly open industry, deeply involved in global supply chains, and has a significant presence of foreign direct investment (FDI) enterprises.
 According to Ms. Do Thi Thuy Huong, Vice President and General Secretary of the Vietnam Electronics Industry Association (VEIA), businesses need to invest in automation, digitalization, artificial intelligence (AI), product design, data management, quality control, and research and development. These factors help transform imported machinery, technology, and raw materials into higher productivity, new products, and greater added value, instead of merely serving low-margin processing stages.
 Along with technological capabilities, developing supporting industries is a crucial condition for reducing dependence on external supply sources. When the country cannot produce the necessary components, materials, molds, equipment, and technical services, the greater the scale of production, the greater the need for imported inputs.
 Therefore, expanding production needs to go hand in hand with developing the domestic supplier ecosystem. Ms. Huong assessed that the Government- approved Program for the Development of Supporting Industries for the period 2026-2030 is an important direction to enhance domestic production capacity, increase the localization rate, and promote Vietnamese businesses to participate more deeply in the global supply chain.
 Another issue is increasing linkages between Vietnamese businesses and the FDI sector. FDI corporations not only bring capital but also technology, management standards, quality control systems, and international market networks. By becoming qualified suppliers, Vietnamese businesses have the opportunity to improve their production capacity and participate more deeply in global supply chains.
 However, connecting supply and demand should not stop at meetings and business introductions. It is necessary to clearly identify what products, components, materials, or processes FDI corporations need; and what capabilities domestic businesses lack to meet those needs. Based on that, management agencies, associations, and business support organizations can then design appropriate programs.
 Besides production capacity, meeting international standards is an increasingly important requirement. Electronics businesses must not only compete on price and quality but also meet requirements regarding the environment, carbon emissions, traceability, chemicals, labor, and environmental, social, and corporate governance (ESG).
 According to Ms. Huong, Vietnam's supporting industries not only need to produce components but also create products that meet international standards, comply with green requirements, and are traceable.
 According to the speakers, improving the quality of import and export growth needs to be considered in relation to the production capacity and ability of Vietnamese businesses to participate in value chains. Importing machinery and raw materials is necessary to maintain and expand production, but long-term effectiveness depends on the ability to master technology, develop supporting industries, improve the quality of suppliers, and meet international standards.
 When domestic businesses can supply more standardized inputs, participate more deeply in the production chain, and gradually take on higher-value stages, the growth of exports and imports will have more impetus to transform into competitiveness and value-added created domestically.

Export-oriented businesses are urgently completing orders for 2026 while preparing to sign additional orders for 2027. Government departments and agencies are also implementing various solutions to support and promote export activities.
For the business community, the final months of the year are a crucial time to achieve growth targets and create a transition to the new year 2027 with higher expectations for export activities.
Since the beginning of the year, Danang Rubber Joint Stock Company (DRC) has focused on expanding production of PCR/LTR tires and all-steel radial tires; while also promoting research and development of new products serving the fields of deep-water ports, railways, and infrastructure construction. Currently, DRC's products are exported to 50 countries and territories. Besides expanding domestic and international markets, the company is also committed to developing green production, researching new factory projects, and strengthening its participation in industrial supply chains.

Another difficulty is the limited internal capacity of export businesses, especially in brand building, international marketing, cross-border e-commerce, and negotiation skills with importers...
Supporting key industries and markets.
According to the Department of Industry and Trade's report, in the last months of the year, the department intensified its efforts to promote and support export businesses in effectively exploiting key markets such as the US, Japan, South Korea , China, EU countries, and Muslim-majority countries; while also boosting trade promotion and making good use of new generation free trade agreements (FTAs) such as the Vietnam-EU Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA) and the Comprehensive and Progressive Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) to penetrate larger markets more deeply.
In addition, focus on supporting businesses in overcoming difficulties related to capital, premises, and traceability of origin; support in resolving inventory issues in the processing and manufacturing industries, and reducing production cost pressure due to price fluctuations.
According to Mr. Huynh Xuan Son, Deputy Director of the Department of Industry and Trade, in addition to general and long-term strategic solutions, the industry and trade sector is also focusing on specific solutions to promote export activities at the end of the year, such as focusing on supporting specific product groups and key export markets of the city.
Specifically, for key markets such as the United States , Japan, and the EU, the department focuses on supporting businesses with documentation proving legal origin, origin control procedures, and trade defense measures. These are crucial factors and conditions that help businesses meet the increasingly stringent requirements of export markets and take advantage of opportunities from free trade agreements.
For key export sectors of the city such as wood and wood products; textiles and footwear; relevant departments and agencies are focusing on updating consumer trends, ecological standards, labor standards, sustainable supply chains, and connecting with major distribution systems and specialized importers to enhance the effectiveness of business connectivity.

For export products such as processed agricultural products, food, OCOP products, and goods from traditional craft villages, these are identified as product groups with great potential in ASEAN, EU, China , and the Middle East markets. articles.full_text:
The EU's Maros Sefcovic said the understanding would "moderate China's export of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the EU".
"This opens the prospect of cutting China's export by more than a half" based on projections over a four-year period, he told reporters after the talks.
"By this step, we're actually preventing several millions of cars exports from China to the European Union," he said.
The critical automotive sector was a focal point in the lead-up to talks, as cheaper products coming from China have strangled European industry and Brussels has sought to manage those exports.
Europe's main auto group welcomed the deal as "a positive step in easing trade tensions".
"Today's announcement can help facilitate the transition to a new era of Chinese presence in the European market in an orderly way and this is in the long-term interests of all parties," Sigrid de Vries, director-general of the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association, said in a statement.
"CRUCIAL FIRST STEP"
The EU trade deficit with China runs at around one billion euros ($1.1 billion) every day.
"It's a crucial first step, but only a first step in the process of rebalancing," Sefcovic told reporters, adding that "dialogue needs results, and where the dialogue cannot deliver, the EU will use its tools to ensure a rebalancing".
In a move that will bring further relief to Brussels, Beijing also committed to continuing the supply of vital items such as rare earth minerals to the European Union.
China is "willing ... to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU", the joint statement said.
While they acknowledged "differences", the two sides said they were committed to maintaining trade and to hold another meeting in March.
The talks follow months of rising tensions between the 27-nation EU and the Asian powerhouse that threatened to escalate into a trade war.
Many in Europe accuse China of unfair trade practices, including supporting firms with huge subsidies, price dumping and currency manipulation.
Europe can ill afford to anger Beijing, but the stakes are also high for China, which is heavily reliant on exports to compensate for its weak domestic economy.
The EU parliament's trade committee chief, Bernd Lange, said ahead of Sefcovic's trip that this "economic crisis in China" gives the bloc "bargaining power".
NEED FOR PREDICTABILITY
"They fully support that that needs to be addressed, but they want it to be done in a proportionate, specific and negotiated way so that we can manage the overall relationship," he said.
Beijing's commitment to continue providing rare earths will bring some comfort to European companies in China, who face complicated access to the critical materials under new rules imposed by Beijing last year in retaliation against tariffs announced by US President Donald Trump.
"Having a bit more transparency and predictability around that" is a key deliverable from this week's talks, Dunnett said.

articles.title: Solving the interest rate problem to support 10% GDP growth. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Solving the interest rate problem to support 10% GDP growth.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
To achieve the 10% GDP growth target, growth in the fourth quarter of 2026 needs to exceed 12.5%. Reasonable interest rates will help businesses feel secure in their operations and ease consumer spending restrictions.
A 10% GDP growth rate, in addition to public investment, depends on many factors such as business investment and consumer purchasing power.
Achieving 10% GDP growth in the face of interest rate challenges.
The final months of the year are when businesses accelerate the import of raw materials and stockpile goods to serve domestic consumption and exports. However, rising interest rates have become a difficult problem for many businesses.
Mr. Tran Van Linh, Chairman of the Board of Directors of Thuan Phuoc Seafood and Trading Joint Stock Company, said that the impact of high interest rates not only affects businesses but also spreads throughout the entire supply chain.
When suppliers of raw materials and materials, as well as partners, also have to borrow at higher interest rates, the financial costs can be passed on to the selling price of goods and services. This places an additional layer of cost on top of the interest payments incurred by manufacturing businesses.
"But businesses can't pass on the increased costs to customers. They'll immediately complain," Mr. Linh said.
High interest rates not only affect businesses but also impact people's purchasing power. Rising mortgage interest rates force many families to tighten their spending, except for essential goods.
Slowing consumer demand can make it difficult for businesses to increase revenue, thereby impacting decisions to increase production, hire workers, and make new investments.
If this situation persists, businesses face a choice: scale back production to preserve profits or accept reduced profit margins to maintain operations and keep jobs for workers.
Fortunately, he observed that most businesses chose the second option, accepting reduced profits and sharing the difficulties with partners while waiting for interest rates to cool down.
GDP in the fourth quarter increased by 12.51%, production and business activities must accelerate.
According to the General Statistics Office, GDP in the third quarter of 2026 increased by 9.95% year-on-year, bringing the growth for the first nine months of the year to 9.01%.
To achieve the full-year growth target, Kafi Securities' analysis team estimates that Q4 GDP needs to grow by approximately 12.51%, meaning investment, construction, and consumption must continue to accelerate.
Mr. Vo Kim Phung, Head of Analysis Department at BETA Securities, told Tuoi Tre newspaper : interest rates are very important to investment and business decisions.
You may also like
For businesses, high interest rates increase financing costs, which in turn affects profitability, cash flow, and the ability to undertake new projects.
For households, rising interest rates on loans for home purchases, car purchases, or other consumer goods can reduce demand for consumption and investment…
Mr. Nguyen Quang Thuan, General Director of FiinRatings, also pointed out that economic growth is maintaining a high level, but the current macroeconomic context limits the room for interest rate reductions.
Foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows and accelerated manufacturing activity continue to support growth.
However, the high demand for imports to support investment and production has led to a trade deficit, while inflation is approaching the target level.
These developments put more pressure on interest rate management. Besides supporting growth, monetary policy must also consider exchange rate stability, inflation control, and ensuring the liquidity of the banking system.
According to FiinRatings' forecast, capital costs in Q4 2026 may remain flat instead of decreasing.
Diversifying funding sources is an urgent necessity.
In the context of public investment continuing to play a crucial role in driving economic growth, there is a need to mobilize large amounts of capital.
According to FiinRatings, the public sector's borrowing needs for the period 2026-2030 will reach VND 6,497 trillion for the central government and VND 622 trillion for local governments.
With the increasing demand for capital from the government , local authorities, and the business sector, competitive pressure for medium and long-term funding may intensify.
According to SGI Capital, many home and auto loans, after enjoying low interest rates recently, have seen a sharp increase, rising to 13-16% per year.
Many people borrow money from banks to buy houses or invest in real estate, believing that interest rates will remain low for many years and house prices will never fall.
Therefore, they lack the financial reserves for a scenario where interest rates rise, or even double after the grace period ends, while rapidly falling house prices make them difficult to sell.
There is a tendency for debt repayment pressure to exceed the cash flow earned by some households.
Therefore, diversifying fundraising channels, especially international sources of capital, is becoming increasingly urgent.
According to FiinRatings, the Ministry of Finance is also studying the option of issuing $1 billion in 10-year government bonds. If implemented, this would be the first international government bond issuance since 2014.
Meanwhile, banks have also raised foreign capital through development finance institutions (DFIs) and syndicated loans. However, access to international capital does not necessarily mean the ability to raise capital at low cost.
On September 16th, the US Federal Reserve (Fed) raised interest rates by 0.25 percentage points, bringing the interest rate range to 3.75-4%. This development, along with the outlook for US monetary policy, continues to be a factor to consider regarding the cost of raising capital in USD.
You may also like
In addition, Vietnam's national credit rating remains below investment grade, with a BB+ rating from Fitch Ratings and a Ba2 rating from Moody's.
In this context, the goal of upgrading the national credit rating to investment grade by 2030 is of significant importance.
Mr. Thuan stated that achieving an investment-grade credit rating could contribute to reducing the cost of capital mobilization, expanding the investor base, and facilitating access to long-term capital from international markets for the government, banks, and businesses.
This is a necessary step to alleviate pressure on domestic capital mobilization, thereby supporting the goal of maintaining reasonable interest rates.
A new interest rate level has been established.
According to data from the State Bank of Vietnam, as of September 30, 2026, outstanding credit in the entire system reached VND 20.75 million billion, an increase of 11.59% compared to the end of 2025 and an increase of 16.69% compared to the same period last year.
Thus, the economy will have gained approximately 2.2 trillion VND compared to the end of 2025.
The State Bank of Vietnam's leadership stated that they will continue to maintain the current policy interest rates, creating favorable conditions for credit institutions to access low-cost capital from this source.
At the same time, commercial banks are required to reduce deposit interest rates for new transactions with maturities of 6 months or more.
The pace of interest rate increases is currently slowing down, and interest rates are essentially hovering around a new level.

articles.title: Between Opportunity And Constraint: ASEAN’s Engagement With An Expanding BRICS - Analysis - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: Between Opportunity And Constraint: ASEAN’s Engagement With An Expanding BRICS - Analysis  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways:
- The 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi under India’s “non-Western, but not anti-West” chairship expanded the platform’s weight, with 11 full members and 10 partners representing roughly half the world’s population and about 45 percent of global GDP at PPP, while inviting ASEAN and other regional bodies to amplify Global South priorities on technology, supply chains and inclusive growth.
- Philippine President Marcos Jr., attending as ASEAN Chair and outreach participant, restated the region’s principles of sovereignty, international law, peaceful dispute settlement, maritime cooperation and supply-chain resilience, securing symbolic visibility inside a forum shaped by China, Russia and other emerging powers without formally aligning the Philippines with BRICS.
- ASEAN’s internal divisions over Myanmar, border and maritime disputes (including the South China Sea), and divergent approaches to China and the United States prevented a unified negotiating position; the article concludes that presence yielded modest hedging value and a seat at the table, but lasting leverage requires greater internal cohesion so that ASEAN can speak with one consequential voice.
Introduction and background
Hosted under India’s Chairship, the BRICS (Brazil, Russian Federation, India, China, and South Africa), an informal intergovernmental organization composed of major emerging and developing economies that acts as a geopolitical and economic counterweight to Western-led institutions like the G7 (world’s major advanced economies composed of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan United Kingdom, and the United States), International Monetary Fund (IMF), and World Bank (WB), held its 18th Summit of Leaders (1) in New Delhi, India on 12-13 September 2026.
Expanding to 11 members from the original four (4) in 2006, with the official inclusion of South Africa in 2010, transitioning the group’s name from BRIC to BRICS, and further enlarging its members in 2024 with Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, United Arab Emirates (UAE), and Saudi Arabia (2) joining, followed by Indonesia in 2025, it aims to challenge the dominance of Western nations in global governance and create a more equitable, multipolar world order. Collectively, BRICS’s has outperformed the developed blocs like the G7. The former’s GDP, adjusted for Purchasing Power Parity (PPP), is over US$88 trillion in 2026 in contrast to the latter’s US$62 trillion). This corresponds to 40% of global GDP,
In addition, BRICS’s 10 partner countries participated in the Summit – Belarus, Bolivia, Cuba, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan, and Vietnam – with a combined GDP at PPP of approximately US$10.46 trillion, hence a total contribution of US$98 trillion GDP at PPP (approximately 45% share to world’s GDP) to global wealth coming from less developed countries. The combined population of these 21 countries – which together comprise the full expanded BRICS alliance of 11 full members and 10 partner nations – is approximately 4.60 billion people in 2026. According to official UN demographic data and Worldometer estimates, this block accounts for roughly 48.5% to 50% of the entire global population.
Moreover, major regional developing blocs – including the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), Eurasian Economic Union (EEU), the African Union (AU), the Latin America and the Caribbean (CELAC), the Gulf Cooperation Council, (GCC), and the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC) (3) – similarly took part in the Summit’s Outreach/Plus sessions. Apart from these groupings, heads of international organizations like the UN’s General-Secretary, Directors-General of the World Health Organization (WHO) and the World Trade Organization (WTO), and Presidents of the New Development Bank (NDB) and Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) respectively were invited to engage and respond to common developing-world challenges.
India framed its chairship theme as “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability,” with the central objective to deepen cooperation among the expanded BRICS membership in three broad areas: political and security cooperation; economic and financial cooperation; and development, technology and people-to-people cooperation. Its 140-paragraph “New Delhi Declaration,” explicitly reaffirmed BRICS’s objective of strengthening a more representative and multipolar international order and increasing the voice of emerging-market and developing countries in global governance.
Importantly, BRICS Chair and Indian Prime Minister Modi clarified that BRICS 2026 “is non-Western, but not anti-West.” India particularly sought to keep BRICS as a platform for cooperation among developing and emerging economies rather than turning it into a military or ideological bloc. This was evident in the declaration’s emphasis on sovereignty, consensus, multilateralism and cooperation.
ASEAN at BRICS Summit: Potential and Limits
As ASEAN Chair of the 2026 48th and 49th Summits, Philippine president Marcos Jr. was requested to be present at the BRICS Summit as well as asked to attend its open sessions (4) as an “outreach country,” i.e., a non- member nation in BRICS’s dialogues. ASEAN, together with other regional organizations of developing countries and multilateral development agencies were entreated to join the open sessions to amplify the voice of the Global South in advancing technological cooperation, including emerging fields like artificial intelligence, fintech (financial technology), and digital public infrastructure. Sessions were also trained to discuss strategies for reducing vulnerability to external economic shocks, strengthening supply chains, and promoting an inclusive approach to global growth for the developing world.
Marcos Jr. on his part presented himself primarily as the representative of ASEAN with a population of almost 700 million people, rather than as a leader attempting to move the Philippines toward BRICS. In his short speech at the BRICS’s open session, he described ASEAN as an open, inclusive and outward-looking community. What is more, he emphasized the region’s three (3) main priorities: peace and security; prosperity corridors; and people empowerment. He argued for: ASEAN centrality; peaceful settlement of disputes; international law; maritime cooperation; disaster preparedness; climate security; supply-chain resilience; food and energy security; responsible use of new technologies; and fairer global governance. This was quite significant politically because it allowed Manila to put an ASEAN voice into a forum increasingly dominated by China, Russia and other emerging powers.
On the positive side, ASEAN’s participation through Marcos Jr’s chairship, he was able to articulate ASEAN’s long-standing principles: respect for sovereignty, adherence to international law, and the importance of consensus-based diplomacy. They subtly counterbalance the assertive behaviour of some BRICS members – particularly China – while avoiding direct confrontation. In this sense, Marcos exemplified ASEAN’s normative framework that is anchored in stability and predictability, even as the region navigates intensifying geopolitical competition.
In an era of fluid alignments, smaller and middle powers must navigate a complex geopolitical landscape without being subsumed by great-power competition. ASEAN attendance to the BRICS summit is an exercise in strategic autonomy and pragmatic engagement; it was utilized to safeguard regional economic interests and advance ASEAN’s core priorities. It is a strategy rooted in hedging. (5) It is also in recognition of the evolving institutional architecture of the Global South. And ASEAN must be present in the rooms where new norms are being shaped. Indeed, the 2026 BRICS Summit was a stage for emerging powers to articulate the vision of a fairer global order. Marcos Jr.’s presence did not transform that vision, but it ensured that ASEAN’s voice was part of the conversation.
Nonetheless, aforesaid positive outcomes must be weighed against the structural limitations that define ASEAN’s position at BRICS. ASEAN’s internal divisions – over Myanmar’s military junta, border dispute between Cambodia and Thailand, territorial claim between Malaysia and the Philippines, maritime and border overlaps between Indonesia and Malaysia, dispute over the South China Sea involving five (5) Southeast Asian countries, China, and Taiwan, over how to balance relations with China and the United States – are not incidental; they are constitutive of ASEAN’s identity as a consensus-based organisation.
The ASEAN is not a monolithic region. In 2026 its fault lines are more visible than ever. These are not abstract disagreements; they shape how member states approach external partners. Indonesia, for instance, is now a full BRICS member, while Malaysia and Vietnam participate as BRICS partners. Their decisions to engage with BRICS reflect a calculated strategy of balancing power and maximising economic opportunities in an increasingly polarised global system – a strategy that does not necessarily align with Manila’s more confrontational approach toward China. When ASEAN speaks at BRICS, it does so with a voice that is fractured, and potential interlocutors know it.
The Philippines’ ASEAN chairship, rather than transcending these divisions, has accentuated them. Manila’s assertive posture toward China may resonate with some member states, but it alienates others who prefer a more conciliatory approach. Undeniably, Southeast Asian states have different security interests, economic dependencies and historical relationships with Beijing, Washington, Moscow and New Delhi. Phnom Penh (VNA) - Prime Minister Le Minh Hung and his Cambodian counterpart Hun Manet co-chaired the Vietnam-Cambodia Business Forum 2026 in Phnom Penh on the afternoon of October 9. 
Jointly organised by Vietnam’s Ministry of Finance in coordination with the Council for the Development of Cambodia (CDC), Cambodia’s Ministry of Commerce and the Vietnamese Embassy in Cambodia on the occasion of PM Hung’s official visit to Cambodia, the event brought together leaders of ministries, sectors and localities, along with around 300 business representatives from both countries. 
Data released at the forum showed that bilateral trade reached approximately 11.4 billion USD in 2025, up more than 12% year on year, and nearly 8.7 billion USD in the first eight months of 2026. Vietnam is Cambodia’s largest trading partner within ASEAN and its third-largest globally. Leaders of the two countries have agreed to work towards raising bilateral trade to 20 billion USD in the near future. 
Vietnam currently has 223 investment projects in Cambodia, with total registered capital of around 3.4 billion USD, spanning agriculture, telecommunications, finance and banking, aviation, food processing, trade and services. Cambodian businesses, meanwhile, have 50 projects in Vietnam with total investment capital of 81.6 million USD. 
Many Vietnamese businesses have maintained a long-term presence in Cambodia in sectors including agriculture, telecommunications, finance and banking, aviation, food processing, trade and services. Besides achieving positive business results, they have created tens of thousands of jobs, contributed to state budget revenues and actively participated in local social welfare activities. 
Addressing the forum, PM Hung stressed that Vietnam and Cambodia are close neighbours and affirmed that, guided by the motto of “good neighbourliness, traditional friendship, comprehensive cooperation and long-term sustainability”, bilateral relations have continued to grow closer, more comprehensive, positive and effective. 
He said that economic, trade and investment cooperation constitutes an important pillar of bilateral ties, which has achieved positive results. However, considerable room remains for further expansion to match the strong political ties and the potential of both countries. 
He held that Vietnam and Cambodia need to demonstrate determination to increase the scale of investment projects, promote infrastructure and logistics connectivity, and simplify and facilitate procedures, as proposed by businesses. 
He noted that Vietnam is entering a new stage of development and implementing comprehensive measures to renew its growth model, with science and technology, digital transformation, innovation and improved human resource quality serving as the foundation for strengthening economic capacity, productivity and competitiveness. 
Vietnam is accelerating institutional reforms and regards the private sector as one of the most important drivers of the economy. The country is determined to achieve double-digit economic growth in the 2026-2030 period and become a high-income developed country by 2045, he said.
Briefing participants on Vietnam’s recent socioeconomic achievements, PM Hung spoke highly of Cambodia’s development progress and the marked improvement in its investment and business environment. 
He emphasised the strong complementarities between the two economies. Cambodia has advantages in land resources, agriculture, raw materials, a young workforce and access to international markets. Vietnam, meanwhile, has processing capabilities, seaports, logistics infrastructure, experience in international economic integration and a network of more than 60 free trade agreement partners. 
“If we establish effective links, one country’s advantages can become opportunities for the other. The resources of both countries can generate highly competitive shared value chains and reach regional and international markets. The target, agreed upon by the leaders of both countries, of raising bilateral trade to 20 billion USD in the near future is entirely feasible and within reach, provided that our governments and businesses are determined to act together,” he said. 
To elevate bilateral economic cooperation to a new level commensurate with the current positive political relationship, PM Hung proposed a number of major orientations. 
First, the two Governments, as well as ministries and sectors of the two countries should further align institutions and policies. They should review and continue simplifying investment, land, immigration, customs and quarantine procedures, while maintaining regular government-business dialogues at least once a year, either at government leadership or ministerial level, to ensure that all difficulties are heard and resolved thoroughly and promptly. 
Second, infrastructure connectivity should be strengthened to link markets. Priority should be given to highways, railways and inland waterways connecting the two countries. Progress on the Ho Chi Minh City-Moc Bai-Bavet-Phnom Penh expressway should be accelerated, while border gates, border markets and logistics centres should be upgraded. The two sides should also promote the “single-window, single-stop” model at major border crossings to enable faster and lower-cost movement of goods. 
Third, Vietnam and Cambodia should deepen value-chain cooperation in agriculture and processing. Rather than limiting cooperation to trading raw materials, they should jointly invest in raw material production areas, deeper processing, quality standards and traceability in Cambodia, allowing Cambodian farmers to capture a greater share of added value. 
Fourth, financial and banking connectivity should be expanded, including greater use of local currencies and cross-border QR payments. Conditions should be created for banks in both countries to expand their networks and provide capital to businesses and residents. Vietnamese commercial banks were also urged to step up consideration of lending to Vietnamese enterprises investing in Cambodia. 
Fifth, the two countries should connect new growth drivers, including digital transformation, e-commerce, renewable energy, power grid interconnection, tourism and high-quality human resource training. 
PM Hung emphasised that while the Government creates favourable conditions, businesses are the ones that turn opportunities into results, outlining several messages for the business community. 
First, he called for long-term and responsible investment, urging Vietnamese businesses in Cambodia to strictly comply with local laws, respect Cambodian culture and customs, prioritise local recruitment and training, protect the environment and contribute to host communities. 
Second, he urged businesses from both countries to strengthen links through joint investment, supply chain development, product development and access to third-country markets. Vietnam also encourages Cambodian businesses to invest in Vietnam and leverage its existing infrastructure and network of free trade agreements to connect with regional and global markets. He affirmed that Vietnam’s market of more than 100 million people remains open to Cambodian businesses and goods. 
Third, he called on businesses to compete through quality, technology and sustainability, focusing on projects with high added value, modern technology, environmental benefits and broader economic impact. 
Reaffirming the principle that business growth drives national development, the leader pledged that the Vietnamese Government would continue supporting businesses investing and operating in Cambodia while welcoming and facilitating Cambodian investment and business activities in Vietnam.
Regarding proposals raised by businesses at the forum, the PM tasked Vietnam’s Minister of Finance with coordinating with relevant ministries and agencies, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Vietnamese Embassy in Cambodia to compile all recommendations. Issues within Vietnam’s jurisdiction must be resolved conclusively and reported to the PM, while matters requiring bilateral coordination should be discussed promptly with Cambodian authorities. 
The PM expressed confidence that traditional friendship, strong political trust and the shared determination of both governments and business communities would deliver notable results in bilateral economic cooperation during a new phase of development, contributing to celebrations marking the 60th anniversary of diplomatic relations in 2027. 
PM Hun Manet praised the organisation of the forum, saying the strong participation of businesses from both countries reflected confidence and interest in expanding trade, investment and business cooperation. 
Against rapid and complex regional and global changes, Cambodia and Vietnam continued to pursue closer cooperation and complementarity, he said. Their relationship remained stable and was expanding across trade, investment, tourism, connectivity and people-to-people exchanges. 
Frequent high-level visits and contacts reflected strong political trust and a shared commitment to strengthening good neighbourliness, traditional friendship, comprehensive cooperation and long-term sustainability, while taking economic ties to a new level. 
Congratulating Vietnam on its remarkable progress across various fields, PM Hun Manet said the two countries’ deep-rooted relationship and economic potential made the target of raising bilateral trade to 20 billion USD achievable, with scope to go further. More importantly, he stressed, the quality and depth of economic connectivity between the two countries must improve. 
He also highly valued the presence and positive contributions of Vietnamese investors to Cambodia’s economic development over more than three decades.

articles.full_text:
Factors supporting a reduction in price pressure.
 Reporting at the meeting, Deputy Minister of Finance Tran Quoc Phuong stated that market prices in the first nine months of 2026 generally trended upwards in the first quarter, decreased in the second quarter, and then increased again in the third quarter. This was mainly due to seasonal factors that increased consumer demand during holidays and Tet (Lunar New Year), along with fluctuations in world fuel prices and input material costs. From March onwards, world fuel and energy prices rose sharply, logistics disruptions and increased input costs impacted domestic price levels. The average CPI for the first nine months increased by 4.52% compared to the same period last year, and core inflation increased by 4.26%.
 Against the backdrop of a volatile global economy and the demand for high growth, the Government has identified controlling inflation, stabilizing the macroeconomy, and ensuring major balances as key priorities. The Government and the Prime Minister have directed the synchronized implementation of solutions to manage prices, ensure the supply of essential goods, closely coordinate fiscal and monetary policies, and strengthen inspection and handling of speculative and price manipulation activities. In response to the impact of conflicts in the Middle East causing sharp increases in oil prices and transportation costs, the Government proactively implemented measures to stabilize the market, control prices, and maintain tax and fee exemptions and reductions on gasoline and diesel to alleviate input cost pressures for businesses and individuals. As a result, the domestic commodity market remained largely stable, and the supply was ensured, contributing to inflation control and macroeconomic stability during the first nine months of 2026.
 Entering the fourth quarter of 2026, pressure on price levels remains due to risks from the international energy market, supply chain disruptions, and the need to boost public investment and consumption during the year-end period.
 However, inflationary pressure has been somewhat eased thanks to the continued implementation of tax and fee exemption and reduction policies; proactive and flexible monetary policy management; abundant domestic food supply; and the ability to recover production after natural disasters.
 The Ministry of Finance has updated two inflation scenarios for 2026: an increase of around 4.5% and 4.8%. The State Bank of Vietnam forecasts average inflation in 2026 to increase between 4.5% and 5.0%. International organizations forecast average inflation in Vietnam to increase by approximately 4.2% to 5.5%. 
|  | 
| Deputy Prime Minister Nguyen Van Thang chaired the meeting of the Steering Committee for Price Management. | 
 Price management practices vary across localities.
 Concluding the meeting, Deputy Prime Minister Nguyen Van Thang stated that in the first nine months of 2026, the global economy continued to face numerous uncertainties and risks from supply shocks. Geopolitical conflicts, protectionism, and policy changes in major economies have profoundly impacted supply chains, prices, and international trade. Energy prices continue to be a major risk factor for global price levels. Countries are adjusting their monetary policies cautiously to control inflation.
 These factors contribute to the continued upward trend or continued high prices of many domestic goods and services.
 According to the Deputy Prime Minister , price management across localities is inconsistent. While many localities have controlled prices very well, thereby supporting economic growth, many others have not.
 Regarding the tasks and solutions for managing prices in the remaining months of 2026, the Deputy Prime Minister stated that, according to experts' assessments, the global situation continues to have many unfavorable and unpredictable developments, facing numerous risks, and will continue to have a significant impact on the domestic market and put pressure on the CPI control efforts to achieve the set target.
 Against this backdrop, from now until the end of the year, the Deputy Prime Minister requested that ministries, sectors, and localities continue to coordinate closely, proactively, flexibly, and effectively in managing fiscal policy, monetary policy, and other macroeconomic policies to control inflation, stabilize the macroeconomy, ensure major economic balances, and create room to support growth and enhance the economy's resilience to external shocks. At the same time, they need to proactively monitor domestic and international economic developments closely, and promptly and decisively implement tasks and solutions to reduce the CPI, thereby creating room to support growth. 
|  | 
| Deputy Prime Minister Nguyen Van Thang gave instructions at the meeting. | 
 Implement inspection procedures for price declarations and listings.
 Ministries, agencies, and localities shall manage the prices of goods and services priced by the state according to a suitable roadmap, carefully assessing the impact on the CPI; ensuring harmony between the goals of implementing the market-based roadmap, controlling inflation, and supporting the recovery of production and business. They shall implement inspections of price declarations and listings, especially for essential goods. Strictly handle acts of speculation, hoarding, and price manipulation aimed at illegal profiteering, exploiting natural disasters, storms, floods, and peak holiday seasons to arbitrarily raise prices; require businesses to promptly reduce prices accordingly when input material costs decrease to protect consumer rights. They shall strictly enforce regulations on the public disclosure of income and expenditure at the beginning of the school year, preventing the 발생 of any income outside the prescribed list.
 The Deputy Prime Minister requested that ministries and agencies focus on inspecting and monitoring the areas under their responsibility because "there are times when input prices have decreased, but output prices, service prices, and commodity prices have not decreased correspondingly or have decreased very slowly."
 It is necessary to strengthen communication and provide timely and transparent information on the government's price management policies and price fluctuations of essential goods, thereby guiding public opinion, stabilizing consumer and business sentiment, and controlling inflation expectations; strengthen the dissemination and training on new price regulations, and proactively and urgently implement the process of receiving and declaring prices to promptly collect data for market aggregation, analysis, and forecasting. 
 The State Bank of Vietnam proactively and flexibly manages monetary policy, coordinating closely with fiscal policy, closely monitoring developments in exchange rates, credit interest rates, money supply, and international capital flows to proactively implement solutions to mitigate the impact of imported inflation.
